propositions.text: Once Crown establishes conditions, burden shifts to accused to raise reasonable doubt about breathalyzer reliability.
propositions.quote: once the Crown has established certain conditions, the burden shifts to the accused to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the breathalyzer test results.

propositions.text: If no evidence raises doubt, results presumed accurate and reflect blood alcohol level at testing and material time.
propositions.quote: If there is no evidence raising such a doubt, the results are presumed to be accurate, which is to say that the alcohol level in the breath sample is presumed to reflect the alcohol level in the accused’s blood at the time of testing, and that level is presumed to be identical to the alcohol level in the accused’s blood at the material time.

paragraphs.summary: Court states burden shifts to accused to raise reasonable doubt about breathalyzer reliability; absent doubt, results presumed accurate and reflect blood alcohol level.

propositions.text: Appeal concerns scope of evidence needed to rebut presumptions of accuracy and identity under s. 258(1)(c) Cr. C.
propositions.quote: This appeal concerns the scope of the evidence that must be adduced to rebut the presumptions of accuracy and identity that are applicable to breathalyzer test results under s. 258(1) (c) of the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C‑46 (“Cr. C.”).

propositions.text: Court allowed Crown's appeal, set aside acquittal, ordered new trial, reasons to follow.
propositions.quote: From the bench, the Court allowed the Crown’s appeal from the judgment of the Court of Appeal, set aside the verdict of acquittal restored by the Court of Appeal, and ordered a new trial, with reasons to follow.

paragraphs.summary: Court states appeal concerns evidence scope to rebut breathalyzer presumptions; allowed Crown's appeal, set aside acquittal, ordered new trial.

propositions.text: Since R. v. St-Onge Lamoureux, accused must show malfunction or improper operation casts doubt on breathalyzer reliability.
propositions.quote: Since that decision, it has been settled that to rebut the presumptions in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C., an accused must adduce evidence tending to show that the malfunctioning or improper operation of the approved instrument casts doubt on the reliability of the results (St‑Onge Lamoureux, at para. 52).

propositions.text: New provisions require evidence casting doubt relate directly to deficiencies in instrument maintenance or test process.
propositions.quote: What the new provisions require is that evidence tending to cast doubt on the reliability of the results relate directly to such deficiencies.

propositions.text: Requirement aims to ensure scientific recognition and proper operation of breathalyzer instruments.
propositions.quote: This requirement has two purposes. First, it aims to ensure continued scientific recognition of breathalyzer test results, and second, it promotes the proper functioning and proper operation of instruments in order to prevent the reliability of the results from being compromised (St‑Onge Lamoureux, at paras. 33‑36).

paragraphs.summary: Court explains accused must show malfunction or improper operation casts doubt on reliability; evidence must relate directly to deficiencies; aims to ensure scientific recognition and proper operation.

propositions.text: Accused discharges burden if adduces evidence of improper operation and shows defect tends to cast doubt on reliability.
propositions.quote: The accused’s burden is discharged if the following conditions are met: (i) the accused adduces evidence relating directly to the malfunctioning or improper operation of the instrument, and (ii) the accused establishes that this defect tends to cast doubt on the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: Each condition has theoretical and practical elements: procedure generally required and not followed; defect's purpose and effect on reliability.
propositions.quote: Each of these conditions has a theoretical element and a practical element. Therefore, for the improper operation of the instrument to be established, it must first be found that a specific procedure is generally required (theoretical element), and it must then be shown that the procedure was not in fact followed (practical element). The evidence from which it can be inferred that the defect tends to cast doubt on the reliability of the results must be looked at in the same manner.

paragraphs.summary: Court states accused must show improper operation and defect tending to cast doubt; each condition has theoretical and practical elements.

propositions.text: No need to decide if improper operation established; no evidence defect cast doubt on reliability here.
propositions.quote: Even if we assume, without deciding, that improper operation of the instrument was established here based on failure to complete the 15‑ or 20‑minute observation period, there was clearly no evidence that this improper operation tended to cast doubt on the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal judgment reversed; Superior Court judgment restored ordering new trial.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal’s judgment must be reversed. The Superior Court’s judgment setting aside the verdict of acquittal by the Court of Québec and ordering a new trial must be restored.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no evidence defect cast doubt on reliability; reverses Court of Appeal, restores Superior Court ordering new trial.

propositions.text: On July 12, 2012, respondent stopped, arrested, taken to police station; officers observed him during call to counsel.
propositions.quote: On July 12, 2012, the respondent Marc Cyr‑Langlois was stopped by Constables Boissonneault and Cousineau while he was driving his vehicle... Constable Cousineau observed the respondent through the window while he placed a call to his counsel, which ended at around 1:05 a.m.

paragraphs.summary: Court states respondent was stopped, arrested, taken to station, and observed during call to counsel on July 12, 2012.

propositions.text: First breathalyzer test at 1:08 a.m. showed 157 mg; second at 1:30 a.m. showed 148 mg; both over legal limit.
propositions.quote: At 1:08 a.m., Constable Boissonneault gave the respondent a first breathalyzer test, which showed 157 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood... At 1:30 a.m., Constable Boissonneault administered the second breathalyzer test, which showed 148 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood.

propositions.text: Respondent charged with impaired driving and blood alcohol over 80 mg; only second charge is in issue.
propositions.quote: The respondent was then charged with operating a motor vehicle while his ability to do so was impaired by alcohol and with operating a motor vehicle with a blood alcohol level exceeding 80 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood. Only the second charge is in issue here.

paragraphs.summary: Court states respondent had two breath tests over legal limit and was charged; only blood alcohol charge is in issue.

propositions.text: Trial court agreed to determine if technician breached duty by failing to observe accused for 15 or 20 minutes before tests.
propositions.quote: the parties agreed that the court should begin by determining whether Constable Boissonneault had breached the duty to operate the breathalyzer properly by failing to observe the accused himself for a period of 15 or 20 minutes before administering each test.

propositions.text: Accused argued breach rebutted presumptions, requiring acquittal absent Crown evidence.
propositions.quote: The accused argued that, in such a case, the presumptions were rebutted, which had to lead to his acquittal in the absence of additional evidence from the Crown.

paragraphs.summary: Trial court agreed to determine if technician breached observation duty; accused argued breach rebutted presumptions requiring acquittal.

propositions.text: Trial judge found technician not required to observe accused himself; observation period was not continuous.
propositions.quote: the trial judge found that, while the technician was not required to observe the accused himself, the period during which Constable Cousineau had done so was not continuous.

propositions.text: Trial judge found failure to follow observation procedure sufficient to raise reasonable doubt and acquitted accused.
propositions.quote: his finding that the procedure had not been followed in this case was sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt.

propositions.text: Only technician testified for Crown; trial judge did not refer to additional evidence; Crown had no evidence on first charge.
propositions.quote: Only Constable Boissonneault testified for the Crown... He did not refer to any additional evidence in this regard. He therefore acquitted the respondent of the second charge, and the Crown stated that it had no evidence to adduce on the first charge.

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge found observation duty not required of technician, failure raised reasonable doubt, acquitted accused; only technician testified; no Crown evidence on first charge.

propositions.text: Crown appealed to Superior Court, which allowed appeal, set aside acquittal, ordered new trial.
propositions.quote: the Crown appealed as of right to the Superior Court, which allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment of acquittal and ordered a new trial.

propositions.text: Superior Court found trial judge made fatal legal error in acquitting accused.
propositions.quote: the trial judge did not properly apply the law and made a fatal error of law in acquitting the [respondent].

paragraphs.summary: Superior Court allowed Crown's appeal, set aside acquittal, ordered new trial, finding trial judge made fatal legal error.

propositions.text: Alberta Court of Appeal in So summarized accused's burden to rebut presumptions as showing deficiency and its relation to reliability.
propositions.quote: To rebut the statutory presumptions an accused must establish to the reasonable doubt standard: (a) a deficiency in the functioning or operation of the instrument; and (b) that the deficiency directly related to the reliability of the breath test results.

paragraphs.summary: Alberta Court of Appeal summarized accused's burden to rebut presumptions as showing deficiency and its relation to reliability.

propositions.text: Respondent sought and was granted leave to appeal to Court of Appeal on question of law.
propositions.quote: The respondent subsequently sought leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal on a question of law, which was granted.

propositions.text: Majority of Court of Appeal set aside Superior Court judgment, restored acquittal verdict.
propositions.quote: A majority of the Court of Appeal set aside the Superior Court’s judgment and restored the verdict of acquittal.

propositions.text: Accused must show improper operation and evidence tending to show it could influence result to rebut presumptions.
propositions.quote: All of the judges agreed that an accused must not only establish that the breathalyzer was operated improperly, but must also adduce evidence tending to show that its improper operation “[could] influence the result” (paras. 38 and 69 (CanLII)).

propositions.text: Majority found determination of doubt was factual and Superior Court erred in intervening absent unreasonable evidence assessment.
propositions.quote: the majority found that this determination essentially concerned a question of fact and that the Superior Court had erred in intervening absent an unreasonable assessment of the evidence by the trial judge.

propositions.text: Dissenting judge would have upheld Superior Court decision for lack of evidence showing deficiency affecting result.
propositions.quote: The dissenting judge would have upheld the Superior Court’s decision on the ground that “[t]he [Court of Québec] judge was not faced with evidence showing a deficiency [that could] affect the result” (para. 71).

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal majority restored acquittal, requiring evidence improper operation could influence result; dissent upheld Superior Court for lack of such evidence.

propositions.text: Issue is how accused can show defect tends to cast doubt on reliability when instrument operated improperly.
propositions.quote: The only real issue is how, in cases where there is evidence that an instrument was operated improperly... the accused can show that this defect tends to cast doubt on the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: Dispute centers on whether purely theoretical evidence suffices to raise reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: The heart of the dispute comes down to the following: is evidence that is purely theoretical sufficient for this purpose?

paragraphs.summary: Court identifies issue: whether purely theoretical evidence suffices to show defect casts doubt on reliability when instrument operated improperly.

propositions.text: Abstract evidence alone unlikely to meet reasonable doubt requirement; concrete evidence usually required.
propositions.quote: While it is not impossible that abstract evidence alone may sometimes meet the requirement of raising a reasonable doubt about the reliability of results, it is more likely that evidence that relates more concretely to the facts in issue will be required.

propositions.text: Here, without concrete evidence, accused's argument was speculative and failed reasonable doubt test.
propositions.quote: without such evidence, the accused’s argument was in the realm of speculation and could not satisfy the reasonable doubt test (St‑Onge Lamoureux, at paras. 52‑53).

paragraphs.summary: Court states abstract evidence unlikely sufficient; here accused's argument was speculative and failed reasonable doubt test.

propositions.text: Disagrees with respondent that theoretical possibility suffices; mere hypothetical possibility insufficient to raise reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: I do not agree with the respondent’s argument that it was enough in this case to show that the procedural defect in issue could, in theory, compromise reliability. Relying on such evidence amounts to accepting a “mere hypothetical possibility”, which is clearly not sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt (R. v. Lifchus, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 320, at para. 30).

propositions.text: Respondent was searched twice, monitored, and test results consistent, so digestive issue would have affected both tests similarly.
propositions.quote: Moreover, it is important to remember that the respondent was searched twice, that he was monitored by the police officers and that the two test results were consistent, which means that if there was a digestive issue that had a distorting effect, it must have occurred before each test and affected each result in the same way.

propositions.text: Improper operation alleged did not tend to show reliability doubt; minimum evidence required was not adduced.
propositions.quote: In this context, the mere improper operation alleged by the respondent did not in itself tend to show that the reliability of the results was in doubt. The minimum evidence required for this purpose was simply not adduced.

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects respondent's theoretical evidence; notes consistent tests and monitoring; finds alleged improper operation did not raise reliability doubt.

propositions.text: Improper operation may alone raise reasonable doubt if serious or closely connected to reliability.
propositions.quote: I do not rule out the possibility that improper operation may be so serious or so closely connected with reliability that it will be sufficient in itself to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results obtained.

propositions.text: Dissenting judge in Court of Appeal said concrete evidence must show improper operation may be linked to results, not mere hypothesis.
propositions.quote: Although expert evidence is not essential, concrete evidence must be tendered to show that the improper operation or malfunctioning of the instrument may be linked to the results (as opposed to the necessity to show that improper operation did in fact lead to unreliable results). In sum, the evidence should not be mere hypothesis or conjecture.

propositions.text: Court of Québec judge pointed to no concrete evidence; Superior Court correctly found no evidence casting doubt on reliability; Court of Appeal majority erred reversing.
propositions.quote: The Court of Québec judge did not point to any concrete evidence in this regard... Zigman J. of the Superior Court correctly found that there was no evidence tending to cast doubt on the reliability of the results, and the majority of the Court of Appeal erred in reversing his decision.

paragraphs.summary: Court states serious improper operation may alone raise doubt; dissent requires concrete evidence; finds no concrete evidence here; Superior Court correct; Court of Appeal majority erred.

propositions.text: Intervener argues accused cannot testify about alcohol consumption or digestive problems without breaching s. 258(1)(d.01) Cr. C.
propositions.quote: An intervener, the Criminal Lawyers’ Association, argues that it would be impossible for an accused to testify about his or her alcohol consumption or digestive problems without contravening s. 258(1) (d.01) Cr. C.

propositions.text: Intervener mistaken; accused can testify about digestive problems to show reliability affected after identifying operation deficiency.
propositions.quote: The intervener is mistaken... an accused who testifies to establish that he or she had a digestive problem is not seeking thereby to show that the instrument was operated improperly. Rather, the accused is providing concrete, rational evidence that the reliability of the results may have been affected, after first identifying a deficiency in the operation of the instrument.

propositions.text: Testimonial evidence about digestive problems is admissible but not compulsory.
propositions.quote: Of course, the fact that such testimonial evidence is admissible does not make it compulsory.

paragraphs.summary: Intervener argues accused cannot testify about digestive issues; court finds intervener mistaken; such testimony admissible but not compulsory.

propositions.text: Respondent denies presenting a 'burping defence' as it relates to s. 258(1)(d.1) Cr. C.
propositions.quote: I do not agree with the respondent, who maintains that he did not present a “burping defence” because that defence relates solely to s. 258(1) (d.1) Cr. C.

propositions.text: Burping defence was essential to respondent's argument that improper operation cast doubt on reliability due to unnoticed digestive issues.
propositions.quote: The burping defence was an essential part of his arguments. He argued that the improper operation of the instrument cast doubt on the reliability of the results precisely because... the police might not notice certain digestive issues that can have a distorting effect.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent denies 'burping defence' but court finds it was essential to his argument that improper operation cast doubt on reliability.

propositions.text: No evidence showed defect cast doubt on reliability; defect cannot form basis for reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: there was absolutely no evidence tending to show that the alleged defect cast doubt on the reliability of the results. That defect therefore could not form the basis for a reasonable doubt.

propositions.text: Acceptance of theoretical evidence based on speculation misinterprets accused's burden; Superior Court did not err in ordering new trial.
propositions.quote: acceptance of theoretical evidence based on speculation reflects a misinterpretation of the accused’s burden of proof, which is an error of law. The Superior Court did not err in setting aside the respondent’s acquittal and ordering a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no evidence cast doubt on reliability; theoretical evidence speculative; Superior Court rightly ordered new trial.

propositions.text: R. v. St-Onge Lamoureux held evidentiary scheme infringes presumption of innocence but justified partly by breathalyzer reliability.
propositions.quote: It was held in R. v. St‑Onge Lamoureux... that the evidentiary scheme applicable to offences involving driving with a blood alcohol level over the legal limit infringes the right to be presumed innocent... One reason why this infringement is justified in part is because of the recognized reliability of breathalyzer test results.

propositions.text: Reliability of breathalyzer results depends on proper functioning and operation; reasonable doubt removes presumptions of accuracy and identity.
propositions.quote: However, the reliability of the results is itself contingent on the proper functioning and proper operation of the instrument. Where an accused raises a reasonable doubt in this regard, there is no longer any basis for the presumptions of accuracy and identity created by s. 258(1) (c) of the Criminal Code... and those presumptions must be discarded.

paragraphs.summary: Prior case held evidentiary scheme infringes presumption of innocence but justified by breathalyzer reliability, which depends on proper operation; reasonable doubt removes presumptions.

propositions.text: Trial judge found technician's testimony showed observation period before breathalyzer was not complied with, raising reasonable doubt about reliability
propositions.quote: the trial judge found that the qualified technician’s testimony tended to show that the observation period required prior to the administration of the breathalyzer test had not been complied with and that this was sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results

propositions.text: Trial judge made no error of law warranting appellate intervention
propositions.quote: In my view, the trial judge made no error of law that would warrant appellate intervention

propositions.text: Issue is weighing of evidence and acquittal must be upheld
propositions.quote: The issue is ultimately one of weighing of evidence, and the acquittal must therefore be upheld

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found technician's testimony raised reasonable doubt; the court finds no legal error and upholds acquittal.

propositions.text: Majority requires evidence that improper breathalyzer operation led to inaccurate results, e.g. accused's physiological reactions
propositions.quote: To require, as the majority does in practice, evidence tending to show that the improper operation of the breathalyzer in fact led to inaccurate results — for example, in this case, by imposing an obligation on the accused to testify about his physiological reactions (such as burping)

propositions.text: Such a requirement would upset balance between accused's constitutional rights and Parliament's objectives
propositions.quote: would upset the delicate balance between the constitutional rights of accused persons and Parliament’s objectives

propositions.text: Recent decision in R. v. Gubbins held breathalyzer maintenance records not available under first party disclosure
propositions.quote: Coupled with the recent majority judgment in R. v. Gubbins, 2018 SCC 44, [2018] 3 S.C.R. 35, which held that breathalyzer maintenance records are not available under first party disclosure

propositions.text: Such a requirement would make defences on which St-Onge Lamoureux's evidentiary scheme depends more illusory
propositions.quote: such a requirement would render even more illusory the defences on which the constitutionality of the evidentiary scheme at issue in St‑Onge Lamoureux depends

paragraphs.summary: The court finds majority's requirement for evidence of inaccurate results disrupts constitutional balance and is undermined by Gubbins decision.

propositions.text: Will discuss St-Onge Lamoureux reasoning, clarify burdens of defence and Crown, consider case facts, and conclude on fairness of new trial
propositions.quote: Therefore, I will briefly discuss this Court’s reasoning in St‑Onge Lamoureux. Then, I will provide some clarification concerning the respective burdens of the defence and the Crown with regard to the functioning and operation of the breathalyzer. I will then consider the facts of this case in order to demonstrate that the original verdict of acquittal is, in my view, unimpeachable. Lastly, I will conclude by emphasizing that it would be unfair to order a new trial given the fact that the Crown is relying on arguments made for the first time on appeal

paragraphs.summary: The court outlines its plan to discuss St-Onge Lamoureux, clarify burdens, analyze facts, and address fairness of a new trial.

propositions.text: Appeal requires considering burden on accused to counter presumptions in s. 258(1)(c) Cr. C. and evidence needed
propositions.quote: Essentially, this appeal requires the Court to consider the burden resting on an accused who seeks to counter the presumptions of accuracy and identity in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. as well as the type of evidence that the accused must adduce to discharge that burden

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appeal concerns the burden and evidence required for accused to counter statutory presumptions.

propositions.text: Position based on majority reasons in St-Onge Lamoureux and recent Gubbins decision
propositions.quote: My position is based, as it was in the recent decision in Gubbins, on the majority reasons in St‑Onge Lamoureux

propositions.text: Majority acknowledges St-Onge Lamoureux but departs from it
propositions.quote: the majority also acknowledges the relevance of St‑Onge Lamoureux, but in my view, and with respect, it departs from that decision

propositions.text: Validity of evidentiary scheme upheld in St-Onge Lamoureux because accused could raise reasonable doubt about breathalyzer operation
propositions.quote: the validity of the evidentiary scheme applicable to offences involving driving with a blood alcohol level over the legal limit was upheld in part in St‑Onge Lamoureux... because there was still a real possibility that the accused could counter the statutory presumptions by raising a reasonable doubt about the proper operation of the breathalyzer

paragraphs.summary: The court states its position relies on St-Onge Lamoureux and Gubbins, finds majority departs from St-Onge Lamoureux which allowed raising reasonable doubt.

propositions.text: Scientific evidence in St-Onge Lamoureux showed breathalyzers reliable but procedures must be followed for accuracy
propositions.quote: Although the scientific evidence adduced in St‑Onge Lamoureux demonstrated the reliability of breathalyzers, it also highlighted the importance of following the relevant procedures faithfully in order to obtain accurate results

propositions.text: Expert evidence shows real possibility of instrument malfunction or improper use during sampling and maintenance
propositions.quote: The expert evidence filed in the instant case reveals that the possibility of an instrument malfunctioning or being used improperly when breath samples are taken is not merely speculative, but is very real

propositions.text: Human error can occur during sampling and maintenance steps of breathalyzers used Canada-wide
propositions.quote: Thus, human error can occur when samples are taken and at various steps in the maintenance of the instruments, which, it should be mentioned, are used Canada‑wide

propositions.text: Hodgson’s report emphasizes importance of proper operation and maintenance for scientifically sound results
propositions.quote: Hodgson’s report, which the prosecution itself relied on as a source of the statutory amendments, refers to the importance of proper operation and maintenance

paragraphs.summary: Prior authority shows breathalyzers are reliable but require faithful procedure following; human error and malfunction are real risks.

propositions.text: Alcohol Test Committee recommends qualified technician observe test subject for 15 minutes before breath sample
propositions.quote: The Alcohol Test Committee (“Committee”) of the Canadian Society of Forensic Science (“CSFS”) has made a series of recommendations... before collecting a breath sample, the qualified technician must, among other things, observe the test subject for 15 minutes

propositions.text: R. v. Drolet cited for similar procedural recommendations
propositions.quote: See also R. v. Drolet, 2010 QCCQ 7719, at paras. 92‑94 (CanLII), cited at para. 35 of St‑Onge Lamoureux

paragraphs.summary: Prior authority recommends a 15-minute observation period by qualified technician before breath sample collection.

propositions.text: Constitutionality depends on whether accused can rebut presumption and how easy it is
propositions.quote: the Court expressly emphasized the fact that the constitutionality of the provisions at issue depended, among other things, on “whether it is possible, and how easy it is, for the accused to rebut the presumption”

paragraphs.summary: Prior court emphasized constitutionality depends on accused's ability and ease to rebut presumption.

propositions.text: Only first requirement of s. 258(1)(c) — adducing evidence of malfunction or improper operation — is reasonable limit on presumption of innocence
propositions.quote: only the first of the three requirements imposed on the accused by s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. — that of adducing evidence tending to show that the instrument was malfunctioning or was operated improperly — constituted a reasonable limit on the right to be presumed innocent

propositions.text: Burden justified because results reliable only if instruments operated and maintained properly
propositions.quote: This burden was justified because it reflected the fact that “the results will be reliable only if the instruments are operated and maintained properly”

paragraphs.summary: Prior court found only adducing evidence of malfunction or improper operation is reasonable burden justified by reliability needs.

propositions.text: Court declined to define nature and scope of evidence to show improper operation
propositions.quote: The Court declined to specifically determine the nature and scope of the evidence required to show that the instrument was operated improperly

propositions.text: Deschamps J. noted relevance of Alcohol Test Committee recommendations for instrument functioning and quality assurance
propositions.quote: Deschamps J. made a point of noting the relevance of the recommendations made by the Alcohol Test Committee of the Canadian Society of Forensic Science

propositions.text: Instruments may not function optimally if suggested procedures not followed
propositions.quote: It can be inferred from these recommendations that the instruments may not function optimally if the suggested procedures are not followed

paragraphs.summary: Prior court noted evidence scope unclear but emphasized committee recommendations and risk if procedures not followed.

propositions.text: Possibility to show procedures not followed means reliability cannot be assumed, justifying burden under s. 1 Charter
propositions.quote: it was possible for the accused to show that the relevant procedures had not been followed — in which case the reliability of the results could not be assumed — that the Court ultimately concluded that the first requirement imposed by s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. was justified under s. 1 of the Charter

propositions.text: This conclusion clarifies burden on accused to counter statutory presumptions
propositions.quote: that conclusion sheds light on the burden resting on an accused who seeks to counter the statutory presumptions

paragraphs.summary: Prior court justified burden because accused can show procedures not followed; court says this clarifies accused's burden.

propositions.text: St-Onge Lamoureux did not elevate committee recommendations to statutory conditions Crown must meet for presumptions
propositions.quote: I am not suggesting that St‑Onge Lamoureux elevated the various recommendations concerning the operation of breathalyzers... to the level of statutory conditions that the Crown must meet to benefit from the presumptions

propositions.text: Only statutory conditions are those imposed by Parliament in s. 258(1)(c)(ii) to (iv)
propositions.quote: The only applicable statutory conditions are those imposed by Parliament in s. 258(1) (c)(ii) to (iv)

paragraphs.summary: The court clarifies only statutory conditions in s. 258(1)(c)(ii)-(iv) apply, not committee recommendations as conditions.

propositions.text: Quebec Court of Appeal majority held accused bears burden to show malfunction or improper operation that could affect reliability, not actual inaccuracy
propositions.quote: an accused who seeks to counter the statutory presumptions bears only the burden of adducing evidence tending to show a malfunction or improper operation of the breathalyzer that could affect the reliability of the results; the accused is not required to show that the results are in fact inaccurate

propositions.text: Evidence need only raise reasonable doubt (St-Onge Lamoureux, Gibson)
propositions.quote: the evidence in question need only raise a reasonable doubt in this regard (St‑Onge Lamoureux, at para. 16; R. v. Gibson, 2008 SCC 16, [2008] 1 S.C.R. 397, at para. 17)

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker and prior authority hold accused must raise reasonable doubt about reliability, not prove inaccuracy.

propositions.text: St-Onge Lamoureux requires evidence of defect that could cast doubt on reliability, consistent with So
propositions.quote: This formulation of the burden is consistent with St‑Onge Lamoureux, which simply requires evidence of a “defect that could cast doubt on the reliability of the results”

paragraphs.summary: Prior authority confirms burden is to show defect that could cast doubt on reliability, consistent with other cases.

propositions.text: Majority and Crown say accused must raise reasonable doubt about reliability by evidence of malfunction or improper operation
propositions.quote: Like the Crown, the majority purports to accept that the burden on the accused is simply to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results by means of evidence tending to show that the breathalyzer was malfunctioning or was operated improperly

propositions.text: Majority requires evidence relating concretely to facts, imposing obligation to cast doubt on accuracy on facts
propositions.quote: Yet by requiring “evidence that relates more concretely to the facts in issue”... the majority is effectively imposing an obligation on the accused to cast doubt on the accuracy of the results on the facts of the case

propositions.text: This is contrary to St-Onge Lamoureux and resurrects second requirement in s. 258(1)(c) Cr. C.
propositions.quote: With respect, I consider it contrary to this Court’s reasoning in St‑Onge Lamoureux to impose such a burden, since it amounts to resurrecting, in attenuated form, the second requirement in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C.

propositions.text: Second requirement to show connection between deficiency and results was serious infringement of presumption of innocence
propositions.quote: this Court held in St‑Onge Lamoureux that this second requirement... constituted a serious infringement of the right to be presumed innocent that could not be justified

paragraphs.summary: The court argues majority wrongly requires accused to show doubt on accuracy, contrary to St-Onge Lamoureux which rejected that burden.

propositions.text: St-Onge Lamoureux requires reasonable doubt about reliability, not accuracy, which have different meanings
propositions.quote: It is no accident that St‑Onge Lamoureux requires evidence that raises a reasonable doubt about the reliability rather than the accuracy of the results. These two terms, though related, do not have the same meaning

propositions.text: Reliability means ability to function without incident; accuracy means conformity to truth
propositions.quote: The former refers, in its technical sense, to the... “ability of a system... to function without incident”... The latter refers to “conformity to the truth”

propositions.text: Court chose to require reasonable doubt about reliability, not accuracy, which is significant
propositions.quote: In St‑Onge Lamoureux, the Court could have required the accused to rebut the presumption of accuracy... Instead, the Court asked the accused to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results. In my opinion, this distinction is significant

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the important distinction between reliability and accuracy and why only reliability doubt is required.

propositions.text: Evidence showing malfunction or improper operation increasing possibility of inaccurate result meets accused's burden
propositions.quote: where the evidence tends to show... that the malfunctioning or improper operation of the breathalyzer increased the possibility of an inaccurate result, then reliability is affected and the accused has met his or her burden

propositions.text: Accused need not tender additional evidence to raise reasonable doubt about accuracy on case facts
propositions.quote: The accused does not have to tender additional evidence in order to directly raise a reasonable doubt about the accuracy of the results on the facts of the case

propositions.text: Sufficient to show recommended procedure not followed and its purpose is to ensure reliability
propositions.quote: In practice, it will be sufficient to adduce evidence tending to show that a recommended procedure was not faithfully followed and that the purpose of the procedure is to ensure the reliability of the results

propositions.text: This is a defect that could cast doubt on reliability within St-Onge Lamoureux meaning
propositions.quote: this is a “defect that could cast doubt on the reliability of the results” within the meaning of St‑Onge Lamoureux

propositions.text: Accused's burden ends there; presumptions justified only if relevant procedures complied with
propositions.quote: The accused’s burden ends there, because the application of the presumptions in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. is justified only insofar as the relevant procedures are complied with

paragraphs.summary: The court states accused meets burden by showing procedure not followed affecting reliability; no need to prove accuracy doubt.

propositions.text: Burden shifts to Crown to prove beyond reasonable doubt deficiency had no impact on accuracy
propositions.quote: The burden then shifts to the Crown to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the deficiency in question had no impact on the accuracy of the results on the facts of the case

propositions.text: Reverse onus on Crown to prove no connection after accused adduces evidence is not excessive
propositions.quote: Deschamps J. noted that there is nothing excessive about this reverse onus: “[B]eing the party that has to prove that there is no connection after the accused has adduced evidence... does not impose a significant additional burden on the prosecution”

propositions.text: If Crown fails burden, it loses benefit of statutory presumptions
propositions.quote: if the Crown fails to discharge this burden, it completely loses the benefit of the statutory presumptions in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C.

propositions.text: Crown should not rely on technician rigour to claim reliability then trivialize it when reliability challenged
propositions.quote: As Mr. Cyr‑Langlois aptly observes in his factum, “[t]he Crown should not be able to rely on the rigour of the technicians to persuade this Court that the results are reliable and then trivialize the importance of that rigour when the reliability of the results is challenged”

paragraphs.summary: The court explains burden shifts to Crown to prove no impact on accuracy; failure loses presumptions; applicant argues Crown inconsistent.

propositions.text: Accused may rely solely on qualified technician's testimony to raise reasonable doubt about reliability
propositions.quote: There is nothing to prevent the accused from relying solely on the qualified technician’s testimony to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results

propositions.text: Evidence to counter presumptions may come from Crown or defence witnesses
propositions.quote: evidence to counter the statutory presumptions may be “sought in depositions given by witnesses of the Crown as well as in depositions of defence witnesses”

paragraphs.summary: The court states accused can rely solely on qualified technician's testimony to raise reasonable doubt, per prior authority.

propositions.text: Qualified technician responsible for proper breathalyzer operation under Criminal Code
propositions.quote: Under the Criminal Code , the qualified technician is responsible for the proper operation of the breathalyzer

propositions.text: Technician's testimony about procedure purpose and failure to follow it can raise reasonable doubt without additional evidence
propositions.quote: Where the technician testifies about a recommended procedure, states that its purpose is to ensure the reliability of the results and, finally, admits that he or she did not follow the procedure faithfully or does not know whether it was followed faithfully, the accused is not obliged to tender additional evidence... to corroborate the technician’s testimony

propositions.text: Such testimony alone can raise reasonable doubt about reliability
propositions.quote: That testimony is in itself evidence that can raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results

propositions.text: Opposite position disregards Parliament's unique role for qualified technicians in blood alcohol analysis
propositions.quote: To take the opposite position would be to disregard the unique role conferred by Parliament on qualified technicians in the context of blood alcohol analysis

paragraphs.summary: The court holds technician's testimony alone can raise reasonable doubt about reliability, reflecting Parliament's role for technicians.

propositions.text: The trier of fact must assess evidence to determine if it suffices to counter statutory presumptions.
propositions.quote: It is for the trier of fact to assess the evidence adduced in order to determine whether it is sufficient to counter the statutory presumptions.

propositions.text: Qualified technician’s testimony alone may not raise reasonable doubt if problems are trivial.
propositions.quote: the trier of fact may well find that, in the circumstances, the qualified technician’s testimony does not in itself raise a reasonable doubt, for example because the problems identified are “frivolous or trivial”

paragraphs.summary: The court states the trier of fact must assess evidence sufficiency to counter presumptions; trivial problems may not raise reasonable doubt.

propositions.text: The trial judge correctly stated the law about accused's burden to show breathalyzer malfunction or improper operation raising reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: The trial judge correctly stated the law. He properly noted that the accused must adduce evidence tending to show that the breathalyzer was malfunctioning or was operated improperly and that the deficiency in question must raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the test taken

propositions.text: Trial judge's factual findings are supported by evidence and verdict of acquittal is unimpeachable.
propositions.quote: His findings of fact on this point are supported by the evidence adduced by the parties. In my opinion, the verdict of acquittal is therefore unimpeachable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge correctly stated law and his factual findings supported; acquittal is unimpeachable.

propositions.text: Crown identified no legal error warranting intervention; deprivation of presumptions was due to concrete evidence of procedural deficiency.
propositions.quote: The Crown has not identified any error of law that would warrant this Court’s intervention. Contrary to what it argues, it was deprived of the benefit of the presumptions ... because of concrete and specific evidence showing that a relevant procedure ... had not been followed

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Crown identified no legal error; deprivation of presumptions was due to concrete evidence of procedural deficiency.

propositions.text: Disagrees with majority that trial judge misinterpreted reasonable doubt or based findings on speculation.
propositions.quote: I cannot agree with the majority that the trial judge misinterpreted the reasonable doubt standard and that his findings were based on “speculation”

propositions.text: Reasonable doubt must relate to improper breathalyzer operation affecting reliability, not just blood alcohol level or accuracy.
propositions.quote: The reasonable doubt simply had to relate to improper operation of the breathalyzer that could affect the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: Evidence in this case was not theoretical regarding improper operation.
propositions.quote: On this point, the evidence adduced in the instant case was not “theoretical”.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees with majority on reasonable doubt interpretation; evidence of improper operation was not theoretical.

propositions.text: Majority concedes improper operation evidence may raise reasonable doubt about reliability in some cases.
propositions.quote: the majority concedes that, in certain circumstances, evidence of improper operation may in itself raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results

propositions.text: Whether evidence suffices to raise reasonable doubt is for trier of fact to decide.
propositions.quote: this is a matter for the trier of fact to decide, since it involves assessing the sufficiency of the evidence

paragraphs.summary: The court notes majority concedes improper operation evidence may raise reasonable doubt; sufficiency is for trier of fact.

propositions.text: Mr. Cyr-Langlois adduced relevant evidence of improper breathalyzer operation; trial judge found it sufficient to raise reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: Mr. Cyr‑Langlois adduced relevant evidence concerning the improper operation of the breathalyzer and the trial judge found that that evidence was sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt

propositions.text: This Court should not intervene in the trial judge's decision.
propositions.quote: This Court should therefore not intervene.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Mr. Cyr-Langlois adduced sufficient evidence; court should not intervene.

propositions.text: Constable Boissonneault testified about a 20-minute observation period to ensure no alcohol consumption or physiological reactions before breath test.
propositions.quote: Constable Boissonneault, the qualified technician, himself stated that the procedures ... include a 20‑minute observation period ... to ensure that the accused has not consumed alcohol, vomited, regurgitated or burped before the breath samples are taken

propositions.text: This testimony sufficed to show a procedure exists to ensure test reliability; no need for training manual or expert corroboration.
propositions.quote: This testimony was more than sufficient to show that a procedure exists for ensuring the reliability of the test results. There was no need to file the training manual ... or to have an expert testify

paragraphs.summary: The court finds technician's testimony about observation period sufficed to show procedure exists; no manual or expert needed.

propositions.text: Cross-examination showed Mr. Cyr-Langlois was not observed continuously during the 20-minute period as required.
propositions.quote: Constable Boissonneault’s cross‑examination also tends to show that Mr. Cyr‑Langlois was not observed during the prescribed period

propositions.text: Boissonneault did not observe accused himself; another officer did but could not confirm continuous observation.
propositions.quote: he had not observed the accused himself ... Another police officer ... did so instead. However ... could not confirm that his colleague had observed the accused continuously

propositions.text: During part of the observation period, accused was alone in a soundproof room exercising right to counsel, so burping could not be determined.
propositions.quote: there was a certain amount of time ... Constable Cousineau was unable to determine whether Mr. Cyr‑Langlois burped, since Mr. Cyr‑Langlois was alone in a soundproof room exercising his right to counsel

propositions.text: Boissonneault was not concerned despite responsibility to ensure no physiological reactions occurred before breath samples.
propositions.quote: Constable Boissonneault does not appear to have been concerned about this, even though he acknowledged that ... he was responsible for ensuring that no physiological reactions occurred

propositions.text: Trial judge could find technician’s testimony sufficient to raise reasonable doubt about compliance with observation period.
propositions.quote: the trial judge could certainly find that the qualified technician’s testimony was sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt about compliance with the prescribed observation period

paragraphs.summary: The court finds evidence showed accused was not continuously observed; trial judge could find reasonable doubt about compliance.

propositions.text: Trial judge could find evidence showed improper breathalyzer operation affecting reliability, not mere possibility of deficiency.
propositions.quote: it was open to the trial judge to find that Mr. Cyr‑Langlois had adduced evidence tending to show improper operation ... and not “simply to show that a deficiency is possible”

propositions.text: This is neither conjecture nor speculation; technician administered tests without following prescribed procedure or ensuring no physiological reactions.
propositions.quote: this is neither “conjecture” nor “speculation” ... the qualified technician administered the tests without faithfully following the prescribed procedure and without ensuring ... no physiological reaction

propositions.text: Trial judge could have reasonable doubt about reliability of results.
propositions.quote: The trial judge could therefore have a reasonable doubt about their reliability.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds trial judge could reasonably doubt reliability due to improper operation, not mere speculation.

propositions.text: Accused discharged burden under s. 258(1)(c) Cr. C. by adducing evidence of improper operation affecting reliability.
propositions.quote: the accused had discharged his burden under s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C.

propositions.text: Quebec Court of Appeal held trial judge was entitled not to extend presumptions to prosecution without further evidence from accused.
propositions.quote: the first instance judge was entitled not to extend the benefit of the presumptions to the prosecution. He did not have to require anything further from the accused.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds accused met burden; Quebec Court of Appeal held trial judge need not require more evidence from accused.

propositions.text: Requiring accused to testify about alcohol consumption and physiological reactions after adducing evidence of improper operation would infringe rights.
propositions.quote: it would be contrary to the right to remain silent and the right to be presumed innocent to require an accused to testify ... when the accused has already adduced evidence tending to show improper operation

propositions.text: Majority's approach shifts burden improperly to accused to observe and testify about physiological reactions.
propositions.quote: the majority’s approach shifts the obligation to the accused to observe himself or herself, make note of every physiological reaction and then testify about this

propositions.text: It is the state's responsibility to ensure compliance with conditions for accurate results, not the accused's.
propositions.quote: It is the state’s responsibility, not that of the accused, to ensure compliance with the requisite conditions for obtaining accurate results.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds requiring accused to testify infringes rights; state must ensure compliance, not accused.

propositions.text: Majority suggests test result consistency shows observation failure had no impact, confirming reliability.
propositions.quote: The majority suggests that the relative consistency of the two test results ... tends to show that failure to comply with the observation period had no impact

propositions.text: Onus is on Crown to prove observation failure had no impact, e.g. by expert testimony.
propositions.quote: the onus was on the Crown to prove it, for example by having the qualified technician or an expert testify on this point

propositions.text: Crown did not prove reliability; presumptions of accuracy and identity no longer justified and must be discarded.
propositions.quote: The Crown did not do so, however, and it must accept the consequences. The application of the presumptions ... was no longer justified, and the presumptions therefore had to be discarded.

propositions.text: Without other evidence of guilt, trial judge had no choice but to acquit Mr. Cyr-Langlois.
propositions.quote: In the absence of any other evidence showing that Mr. Cyr‑Langlois was guilty, the trial judge had no choice but to acquit him.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Crown failed to prove reliability; presumptions discarded; trial judge had to acquit.

propositions.text: Even if Crown's new arguments were accepted, court would hesitate to order new trial due to change in prosecution position.
propositions.quote: I would hesitate to order a new trial in this case. ... the position taken by the prosecution on appeal is clearly different from the one it took at trial.

propositions.text: Intervener Association québécoise des avocats et avocates de la défense points out prosecution's appellate position differs from trial position.
propositions.quote: As pointed out by an intervener, the Association québécoise des avocats et avocates de la défense, the position taken by the prosecution on appeal is clearly different from the one it took at trial.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes prosecution's appellate position differs from trial; would hesitate to order new trial.

propositions.text: Crown prosecutor did not argue at trial that technician's testimony alone was insufficient or that manuals or accused's testimony were necessary.
propositions.quote: The Crown prosecutor never argued before the trial judge that the qualified technician’s testimony could not be sufficient in law ... or that the accused had to testify about his alcohol consumption and physiological reactions

propositions.text: Prosecutor's trial position was that accused was sufficiently observed by officers.
propositions.quote: Rather, the prosecutor’s position was that Constables Boissonneault and Cousineau had observed the accused for a period of time that was sufficient in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Crown did not argue at trial that testimony was insufficient or manuals/testimony necessary; trial position was sufficient observation.

propositions.text: Ordering new trial would give Crown a second chance based on new arguments made first on appeal, violating double jeopardy.
propositions.quote: To order a new trial would therefore be to give the Crown a second chance ... on the basis of arguments that were made for the first time on appeal. ... such a result would be contrary to the double jeopardy principle

propositions.text: Double jeopardy principle prohibits retrying accused based on new arguments first raised on appeal.
propositions.quote: double jeopardy principle (see, for example, R. v. Varga ... R. v. Knight ... R. v. Suarez‑Noa ... R. v. Penno ... R. v. Vaillancourt ... R. v. Patel ... Wexler v. The King)

paragraphs.summary: The court holds ordering new trial on new appellate arguments violates double jeopardy principle.

propositions.text: Trial judge made no reviewable error finding reasonable doubt about improper breathalyzer operation and countering presumptions.
propositions.quote: the trial judge made no reviewable error in finding that Mr. Cyr‑Langlois had raised a reasonable doubt about improper operation of the breathalyzer that could affect the results and that the presumptions ... had therefore been countered

propositions.text: Hogue J.A. held trial judge did not have to require anything further from accused.
propositions.quote: I agree with Hogue J.A. that the trial judge “did not have to require anything further from the accused”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds trial judge made no error; agrees with Hogue J.A. that no further evidence was required from accused.

propositions.text: Majority's approach unduly limits defences based on improper breathalyzer operation that justify evidentiary scheme under s. 1 Charter.
propositions.quote: majority’s approach unduly limits the defences based on improper operation of a breathalyzer that in fact make it possible to justify the evidentiary scheme ... under s. 1 of the Charter

paragraphs.summary: The court finds majority's approach unduly limits defences based on improper breathalyzer operation.

propositions.text: Majority's reasons rely on Crown arguments made first time on appeal; ordering new trial would be inappropriate.
propositions.quote: majority’s reasons are essentially based on arguments that the Crown made for the first time on appeal. It would be all the more inappropriate, in the circumstances, to order a new trial

paragraphs.summary: The court finds majority relies on new Crown arguments; ordering new trial would be inappropriate.

propositions.text: Dismiss appeal; appeal allowed with Côté J. dissenting.
propositions.quote: For all these reasons, I would dismiss the appeal. Appeal allowed, Côté J. dissenting.

propositions.text: Solicitors for parties and interveners are listed.
propositions.quote: Solicitor for the appellant: Director of Criminal and Penal Prosecutions, Québec. Solicitors for the respondent: BMD, Laval. Solicitor for the intervener the Attorney General of Ontario: ...

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses appeal; appeal allowed with dissent; solicitors for parties and interveners listed.
